findings.summary: Page 1 opens with bullets keyed to cause numbers that are only defined by the "The Nine Causes" table on page 2, so the first thing a learner reads is an unresolvable reference.
findings.evidence: Page 1, first block: "4: a missed `cancel()` keeps the timer and child ctx alive until the deadline." … "6: a missing `Done()`, or one skipped by an early `return` before the `defer`." … "9: two goroutines wait on each other, rest of the program is fine." The numbering source appears only on page 2: table rows "4 no `defer cancel()`", "6 `WaitGroup` no `Done()`", "9 mutual blocking".
findings.fix: Swap pages 1 and 2 so the nine-cause table and its per-cause bullets (1,2,3,5,8) come first, with the 4/6/7/9 bullets following on the same or next page; or move the "The Nine Causes" table to the top of page 1 above the numbered bullets.

findings.summary: The caption's first sentence is a series label rather than a hook, burying the actual hook in sentence two.
findings.evidence: "Part 2 of GO GOROUTINES. A goroutine costs 2 KB and about a microsecond — until one blocks forever..."
findings.fix: Open with the hook and move the label to the end: "A goroutine costs 2 KB and about a microsecond — until one blocks forever, and then it costs you a stack, its captured variables, and eventually the pod. ... (Part 2 of GO GOROUTINES.)"

findings.summary: The definition of a goroutine leak sits near the bottom of page 1, after the causes, the fixes and the symptom profile have already been taught.
findings.evidence: Page 1 runs cause bullets → "The Fixes" → "Symptom Profile" → only then "Why The GC Cannot Help": "A leak is a goroutine permanently `_Gwaiting`, unreachable by anything that could finish it."
findings.fix: Move the "Why The GC Cannot Help" heading and its four bullets to the top of the leak section, ahead of the cause list and the fixes, so the definition precedes every use of the word "leak".

findings.summary: The claim that an un-Stopped `time.Ticker` "fires forever" is outdated for Go 1.23+, and contradicts the Go 1.23 timer-GC caveat the same handbook applies to `time.After` on page 7.
findings.evidence: Page 2 table: "5 `Ticker` no `Stop`" / "fires forever"; page 5 tip: "`defer ticker.Stop()` on every `time.Ticker` — otherwise it keeps firing into a channel nobody drains, waking the runtime for nothing." Go 1.23 release notes: "Timers and Tickers ... become eligible for garbage collection immediately, even if their Stop methods have not been called. Earlier versions of Go did not collect unstopped Timers until after they had fired and never collected unstopped Tickers."
findings.fix: Scope the claim the way the `time.After` bullet is scoped: an un-Stopped Ticker keeps firing only while something still references it (e.g. a leaked goroutine ranging over `ticker.C`); since Go 1.23 (module declaring `go 1.23`+, unless `GODEBUG=asynctimerchan=1`) an unreferenced un-Stopped Ticker is collected. Keep `defer ticker.Stop()` as the rule, but drop "fires forever" as an unconditional statement.

findings.summary: `goleak` is shown in code and warned about before the page that says what goleak actually does.
findings.evidence: Page 2 shows "defer goleak.VerifyNone(t)" and the callout "goleak flags library noise … Whitelist them with `goleak.IgnoreTopFunction`" — but the definition arrives only on page 3: "`uber-go/goleak` fails the test if goroutines outlive it. Per test with `VerifyNone`, or once via `TestMain`."
findings.fix: Move page 3's two definitional bullets (what goleak does, VerifyNone vs TestMain) to page 2 immediately above the "Catch It In Tests" code block, leaving the whitelisting callout after them.

findings.summary: Cause 8 is stated in terms of a worker pool and its jobs channel, a pattern that is only introduced four pages later.
findings.evidence: Page 2: "8 jobs never closed | worker `range`" and "8: `range` over the jobs channel blocks after the last job." The pattern is defined only on page 6: "Worker pool: N goroutines ranging one jobs channel, results on a second."
findings.fix: Either move the worker-pool/semaphore/pipeline pattern pages (5–6) ahead of the leak pages, or add one sentence to cause 8 on page 2 defining a worker pool as N goroutines ranging over a shared jobs channel.
Run the fit pass — it adds material from the book without removing anything.

findings.summary: The "Against Other Runtimes" comparison table on page 4 is separated from the bullets that explain its four rows, which land on page 6 after an unrelated patterns page.
findings.evidence: Page 4 table rows: "async/await | no function coloring", "Erlang process | per-process heap", "Thread pool | no queue-head block". Page 6 first block: "async/await: Go's blocking call is not contagious across the API surface. … Erlang: true isolation and supervision trees … Thread pool: no size tuning, but no built-in backpressure either."
findings.fix: Move page 6's four comparison bullets onto page 4 directly beneath the "Against Other Runtimes" table, and let page 6 open with the cost table instead.

findings.summary: Two beginner-audience hashtags are irrelevant to a deep runtime-internals part about scheduler behavior, leak taxonomy, and pprof triage.
findings.evidence: "#codenewbie", "#learntocode" alongside content on "G/M/P, what `schedule()` does 61 ticks at a time" and "the pprof ladder"
findings.fix: Replace #codenewbie and #learntocode with topic-accurate tags such as #pprof and #goruntime.

findings.summary: The "heap flat, RSS up" signature is stated unconditionally even though the same page says each leaked goroutine retains its captured variables, which are live heap objects.
findings.evidence: "RSS climbing while the heap live-set stays flat." and "Heap flat + RSS up = stacks, not objects." versus "Each leaked one holds its stack and every captured variable."
findings.fix: Qualify it: goroutine stacks are accounted in `StackInuse`, not the heap profile, so RSS grows without heap growth only when the leaked goroutines capture little; closures retaining request buffers, responses, or slices also grow the live heap, so a flat heap is a hint, not a requirement.

findings.summary: The yellow sticky note's pushpin graphic sits on top of the last line of the Regression Guard code block, clipping characters in the string literal.
findings.evidence: Code line `t.Fatal("goroutines leaked")}` — the red pushpin of the note "poll with a deadline, not one check" lands on the word `leaked`, cutting through its glyphs.
findings.fix: Shift the sticky note (and its pin) down or right so its bounding box, including the pin, clears the final code line; there is ample empty page below the code block.

findings.summary: The Fan-Out/Fan-In sticky note's pushpin overlaps the closing line of the code block, obscuring part of the call.
findings.evidence: Code line `go func(){wg.Wait();close(out)}()` — the pin for the note "closer runs in its own goroutine" overlaps around `close(out)`.
findings.fix: Move the note/pin anchor below the code block's last baseline (or place the pin at the note's left edge) so no pin pixels intersect the code text.

findings.summary: The semaphore code comments point at `errgroup`'s `SetLimit` before errgroup has been introduced anywhere in the part.
findings.evidence: Page 5 code: "// or: g.SetLimit(8)" with no prior mention of `g` or errgroup; errgroup first appears on page 6: "`errgroup.SetLimit(n)` does the same inside a group" and "`errgroup` propagates the first error and cancels the shared context."
findings.fix: Introduce errgroup before page 5 (move page 6's two errgroup bullets up to the "Bounding The Spawn" section) or drop the `g.SetLimit(8)` comment from the page 5 code block and keep the reference for page 6.

findings.summary: `errgroup.SetLimit` is said to do "the same" as an N-buffered channel semaphore, but SetLimit blocks `g.Go` and therefore bounds goroutine count, not merely parallelism.
findings.evidence: "Buffered channel of size N = semaphore: unbounded goroutines, bounded parallelism." / "`errgroup.SetLimit(n)` does the same inside a group" — while the sidebox on the same page prescribes "Bound it with a pool, semaphore, or `SetLimit`" as the cure for "Unbounded spawning ... A traffic spike becomes an OOM."
findings.fix: Distinguish the two: `SetLimit(n)` makes `g.Go` block until a slot frees, so live goroutines are capped at n; a channel semaphore caps goroutine count only if the acquire happens before the `go` statement — acquiring inside the goroutine bounds parallelism but still lets goroutines (and their stacks) pile up under a spike.

findings.summary: "Same for `main` returning" extends "runs no deferred cleanup in any goroutine" to a normal return from main, which does run main's own deferred functions.
findings.evidence: "`os.Exit` skips everything ... A hard exit runs no deferred cleanup in any goroutine. Same for `main` returning — every other goroutine dies mid-flight."
findings.fix: Split the two cases: `os.Exit` runs no defers at all, including main's; returning from `main` runs main's own defers and then exits the process, killing every other goroutine mid-flight without running theirs.
